clinicalPearls: A sterile autoinflammatory bone disorder of children and adolescents, with recurrent bone pain and swelling but negative cultures
Lesions are frequently multifocal and symmetrical, favouring the metaphyses of long bones, the clavicle, pelvis and vertebrae
Regarded as the paediatric counterpart of SAPHO syndrome, sharing autoinflammatory pathophysiology
Commonly associated with psoriasis, palmoplantar pustulosis and inflammatory bowel disease
Whole-body MRI is the key modality to detect clinically silent lesions and define the multifocal distribution
A diagnosis of exclusion made after infection and malignancy are ruled out, often confirmed by biopsy showing sterile inflammation
Treated with NSAIDs first-line, escalating to bisphosphonates, TNF inhibitors or other DMARDs for persistent or spinal disease
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, also termed chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis, is an autoinflammatory disease driven by dysregulated innate immunity rather than infection. An imbalance between pro-inflammatory cytokines (including interleukin-1, tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-17) and anti-inflammatory signalling leads to sterile osteoclast-mediated bone inflammation with reactive sclerosis and hyperostosis. Genetic contributions are recognised, with monogenic forms such as those involving IL-1 pathway dysregulation informing understanding of the sporadic disease. The process produces recurrent, often multifocal and symmetrical osteitis, and overlaps mechanistically with SAPHO syndrome as part of the same sterile osteomyelitis spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Leukaemia and lymphoma with bone involvement
additionalInvestigations: Whole-body MRI to identify multifocal, often asymptomatic, bone lesions
Plain radiographs showing lytic lesions with surrounding sclerosis and hyperostosis
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), typically normal or mildly elevated
Bone biopsy with microbiology and histology to exclude infection and malignancy
Screening for associated psoriasis, palmoplantar pustulosis and inflammatory bowel disease
redFlags: Systemic features (persistent fever, weight loss, night pain) raising concern for malignancy
Solitary aggressive lytic lesion where sarcoma or infection cannot be excluded without biopsy
Vertebral involvement with collapse or neurological signs
Failure to respond to treatment, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Many children have a self-limiting or relapsing-remitting course with eventual remission, but a substantial minority develop chronic disease; vertebral involvement can lead to fracture and deformity, so early detection and treatment are important.
pitfalls: Treating as bacterial osteomyelitis with repeated antibiotics or surgery despite sterile cultures
Missing additional silent lesions by relying on targeted rather than whole-body imaging
Overlooking vertebral disease that risks compression fracture
Not screening for associated skin and bowel inflammatory conditions
management: First-line non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to control the sterile osteitis and pain
Bisphosphonates (such as pamidronate) for inadequate NSAID response and for vertebral disease to protect against collapse
TNF-alpha inhibitors or conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate or sulfasalazine, with corticosteroids, for refractory or multifocal disease
Whole-body MRI to detect clinically silent lesions and monitor the multifocal distribution
Screening for and management of associated psoriasis, palmoplantar pustulosis and inflammatory bowel disease
Physiotherapy and pain management to maintain mobility and function
Rheumatology-led multidisciplinary care with monitoring for vertebral fracture and deformity
